Behind the route Mathematics & limitations +

The cone unfolds into a sector with angle 120°. The shortest surface path becomes a straight line. Its nearest point to the apex is the highest point of the trip.

For slant height L, radius R, destination distance b = L − offset and separation θ: α = θR/L, D = √(L² + b² − 2Lb cos α). The turning fraction is t = clamp((L² − Lb cos α)/D², 0, 1). Downhill length = (1 − t)D.

“First uphill, then downhill” does not specify one route length. The angle and the meaning of “10 units from the base” matter; here the 10 units are measured along the generator.

Read about cone unfolding ↗

Routes follow edges of a triangulated height grid. Dijkstra finds the minimum sum of edge lengths. “Reduce climbing” minimizes distance + 8 × elevation gain. “Lowest maximum grade” uses a minimax search; it does not minimize distance among equal-grade routes.

The grade limit removes steep edges before search. Results are exact for this graph, approximate for the continuous terrain. Grid orientation and resolution affect the route. All synthetic models and imported data use local coordinates in metres.

Read about shortest-path algorithms ↗

Exploratory planning model. Railway curve radius, earthworks, geology, drainage, vehicle dynamics and engineering standards are outside this version.
